title: CRA Financial Reviewer - Canadian SR&ED Tax Credit Glossary
description: Understand how a CRA Financial Reviewer audits your R&D expenditures and documentation in our Canadian SR&ED tax glossary.
summary: A CRA financial reviewer (FR) is the Canada Revenue Agency reviewer who audits expenditure allowability and investment tax credit calculations in a Canadian SR&ED claim, reporting to a Financial Review Manager. During a review, the FR interviews the claimant's financial personnel; any proposed adjustments arrive in a Proposal Package, and claimants have 30 calendar days to respond.

body.text: A CRA financial reviewer (FR) is the Canada Revenue Agency reviewer who audits expenditure allowability and investment tax credit calculations in a Canadian SR&ED claim, reporting to a Financial Review Manager. During a review, the FR interviews the claimant's financial personnel; any proposed adjustments arrive in a Proposal Package, and claimants have 30 calendar days to respond.

Canada operates one of the world's most comprehensive fiscal incentive frameworks for industrial research and innovation through the federal Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program, a dual-pillar system of income tax deductions and Investment Tax Credits (ITCs), complemented by ten provincial and territorial research and development (R&D) tax credit regimes1. Between December 2024 and November 2026, the Canadian R&D tax landscape underwent its most significant statutory overhaul in over a decade5. At the federal level, the enactment of Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026, codified and expanded the proposals from the December 16, 2024 Fall Economic Statement (FES) and the November 4, 2025 Federal Budget5. Specifically, for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, Parliament doubled the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% refundable ITC from $3,000,000 to $6,000,000 (superseding the interim $4,500,000 proposal announced in the 2024 FES), widened the prior-year taxable capital phase-out thresholds from $10,000,000–$50,000,000 to $15,000,000–$75,000,000, introduced an elective three-year average gross revenue phase-out structure, extended the enhanced 35% ITC to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs), and restored the eligibility of SR&ED capital expenditures, shared-use equipment (SUE), and equipment lease costs for property acquired after December 15, 20242. Concurrently, the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) launched a formal voluntary Pre-Claim Approval process on April 1, 2026, while at the provincial level, Quebec abolished eight legacy R&D tax measures for fiscal periods beginning after March 25, 2025, replacing them with the consolidated 30%/20% refundable Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC), and Saskatchewan doubled its refundable Canadian-controlled private corporation (CCPC) expenditure cap from $1,000,000 to $2,000,0008.
1. Federal Statutory Architecture and the 2024–2026 Legislative Reforms
1.1 Statutory Foundation under the Income Tax Act and Income Tax Regulations

The federal SR&ED Tax Incentive Program is anchored in the Income Tax Act (R.S.C., 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.), hereinafter the "ITA" or the "Act") and Part XXIX of the Income Tax Regulations (C.R.C., c. 945, hereinafter the "Regulations")2. Unlike discretionary government grants that depend on competitive budget envelopes, the SR&ED program is a statutory entitlement embedded within the Canadian self-assessment income tax system. According to CRA program statistics and OECD innovation tax data, the federal SR&ED program distributes between $3.5 billion and $4.5 billion annually across roughly 21,000 claimants, approximately 75% of which are small businesses3. Any taxpayer carrying on a business in Canada that performs qualifying SR&ED work in Canada and submits the prescribed forms containing prescribed information by the statutory reporting deadline is legally entitled to two complementary tax incentives4:

items: First-Pillar Incentive — Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures (Section 37 of the ITA): Under subsection 37(1) of the ITA, a taxpayer carrying on a business in Canada may pool allowable current and (for property acquired after December 15, 2024) capital SR&ED expenditures incurred in Canada that are related to a business of the taxpayer (or, under subsection 37(1.1), related to a business actively carried on by a non-arm's length related corporation)6. Balances in the Section 37 pool may be deducted in full or in part to reduce net business income for tax purposes in the current taxation year, or carried forward indefinitely to offset business income in any subsequent taxation year21.

Second-Pillar Incentive — SR&ED Investment Tax Credits (Sections 127 and 127.1 of the ITA): Under subsections 127(5), 127(9), and 127(10.1) of the ITA, a claimant earns an Investment Tax Credit (ITC) calculated as a percentage (15% basic rate or 35% enhanced rate) of its "SR&ED qualified expenditure pool" at the end of the taxation year2. Under section 127.1, qualifying corporations may receive all or a portion of their unused ITCs as a direct cash refund, while non-refundable ITCs may be applied to reduce Part I federal income tax otherwise payable, carried back up to 3 preceding taxation years, or carried forward up to 20 subsequent taxation years2.

body.text: 1.2 The 2024 Fall Economic Statement, Budget 2025, and Bill C-15 (Royal Assent March 26, 2026)

In auditing Canadian R&D tax documentation prepared between late 2024 and 2026, a vital point of verification involves distinguishing between the initial policy proposals tabled in the December 16, 2024 Fall Economic Statement (FES), the draft legislative proposals released for consultation by the Department of Finance on August 15, 2025, and the final enacted legislation introduced in Budget 2025 (tabled on November 4, 2025 by the Minister of Finance and National Revenue, François-Philippe Champagne) and passed into law via Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 20265.

In the December 16, 2024 FES (and the August 15, 2025 draft legislative package), the federal government initially proposed increasing the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% ITC from $3,000,000 to $4,500,000 (alongside announcing consultations toward a federal patent box regime)5. However, before that $4,500,000 threshold was enacted, Budget 2025 superseded it by increasing the expenditure limit to $6,000,000, retroactive to taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024 (that is, taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024)2. With Bill C-15 receiving Royal Assent on March 26, 2026, the $6,000,000 annual expenditure limit is the binding statutory threshold for all taxation years beginning after December 15, 20242. Any tax advisory report or financial model referencing a $4,500,000 limit for post-December 15, 2024 taxation years reflects superseded pre-Budget 2025 draft proposals and understates the maximum annual enhanced federal ITC by $525,000 ($1,500,000 × 35%)2.

body.text: 1.3 Investment Tax Credit Rates, Refundability Matrix, and Carryover Mechanics

Under subsections 127(9) and 127(10.1) of the ITA, the rate at which a claimant earns SR&ED ITCs and the extent to which those ITCs are refundable in cash under section 127.1 depend on four legal variables: (1) the legal status of the taxpayer (CCPC, ECPC, other corporation, individual/sole proprietorship, trust, or partnership); (2) whether a CCPC meets the definition of a "qualifying corporation" under subsection 127.1(2); (3) whether the qualified expenditures fall within or exceed the taxpayer's annual expenditure limit; and (4) whether the qualified expenditures are of a current nature (including the Prescribed Proxy Amount) or of a capital nature2.

Under the CRA's SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy (updated October 7, 2026), a CCPC is distinguished between a "qualifying corporation" and a "non-qualifying corporation" (other than an excluded corporation) based on its prior-year taxable income and taxable capital thresholds under subsection 127.1(2)2. While both qualifying and non-qualifying CCPCs receive a 100% cash refund on their enhanced 35% ITC earned on current expenditures (and a 40% cash refund on their enhanced 35% ITC earned on capital expenditures), only a "qualifying corporation" receives a 40% cash refund on the basic 15% ITC earned on expenditures exceeding its expenditure limit2. Furthermore, under the post-December 15, 2024 regime, an Eligible Canadian Public Corporation (ECPC) is defined in subsection 127(9) and accesses the enhanced 35% refundable ITC on up to $6,000,000 of qualified expenditures (allocated across consolidated group members under subsection 127(10.6))2. ECPCs access the 35% refundable ITC up to the expenditure limit while earning a non-refundable 15% rate above the limit, and individuals and trusts earn the 15% basic rate with 40% refundability2.

body.text: When a claimant earns an SR&ED ITC in a taxation year, the credit is first evaluated against federal Part I tax otherwise payable under subsection 127(5)2. A claimant may choose how to utilize its ITC subject to applicable rules, and refundable ITCs are paid on the unclaimed balance of ITCs earned in the year2. Under subsection 127.1(3), any ITC refunded to the taxpayer under section 127.1 is deemed to have been deducted by the taxpayer under subsection 127(5) for the year, thereby reducing the remaining ITC balance available for carryback or carryforward2. Any remaining unrefunded and unapplied ITC balance may be carried back up to 3 preceding taxation years under subsection 127(5) to offset Part I tax otherwise payable in those prior years (limited to the lesser of the unused current-year ITC not deductible in the current year and the prior year's Part I tax in excess of ITCs available in that prior year), or carried forward up to 20 subsequent taxation years (applicable to 2008 and later taxation years) to offset Part I tax payable in future years2.

Crucially, SR&ED ITCs are taxable in the subsequent taxation year8. Under paragraph 37(1)(e) of the ITA, the amount of any SR&ED ITC deducted against Part I tax, carried back to a prior year, or refunded in cash in a given taxation year reduces the taxpayer's Section 37 pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures in the immediately following taxation year23. If the taxpayer deducts its entire Section 37 pool in Year 1 (bringing the pool balance to zero at the end of Year 1), the subtraction of Year 1's ITC under paragraph 37(1)(e) in Year 2 creates a negative Section 37 pool balance; under paragraph 12(1)(v) of the ITA, any negative Section 37 pool balance at the end of Year 2 must be included directly in the taxpayer's business income for Year 28. Adding that negative balance into income under paragraph 12(1)(v) simultaneously adds the amount back to the Section 37 pool under paragraph 37(1)(c.1), restoring the opening pool balance to nil (zero) for the following year23.
1.4 Expenditure Limit Phase-Out Formulas: Taxable Capital Method vs. Gross Revenue Election

For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the maximum annual expenditure limit on which a CCPC or ECPC may earn the 35% enhanced ITC is $6,000,000 (prorated by the number of days in the taxation year divided by 365 for short taxation years under subsection 127(10.5))2. Specific rules also apply under subsection 127(10.5) when a CCPC has more than one taxation year ending in the same calendar year and is associated in two or more of those taxation years with another CCPC having a taxation year ending in that calendar year2. The phase-out of the $6,000,000 expenditure limit operates under two statutory methods:
1. The Taxable Capital Method (Default for CCPCs — Subsections 127(10.2) and 127(10.21))

Unless a CCPC files an election under subsection 127(10.31) (or, for associated CCPCs, subsection 127(10.32)) to use the revenue method, its expenditure limit is phased out on a straight-line basis when its taxable capital employed in Canada (as defined in the ITA and referenced in archived Interpretation Bulletin IT-532, Part I.3 – Tax on Large Corporations) for the immediately preceding taxation year—combined with the taxable capital employed in Canada of all associated CCPCs—lies between $15,000,000 and $75,000,0002. For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the statutory formula for the CCPC expenditure limit under the taxable capital method is2:

Expenditure limit = $6,000,000 × [($60,000,000 − A) ÷ $60,000,000], where A is $0 if the prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada of the CCPC (and its associated CCPCs) is ≤ $15,000,000, and A is the lesser of $60,000,000 and the amount by which that taxable capital exceeds $15,000,000 if prior-year taxable capital exceeds $15,000,0002. Consequently, every $10 of prior-year taxable capital above $15,000,000 reduces the $6,000,000 expenditure limit by $1, until the expenditure limit becomes nil at $75,000,000 of taxable capital2. For taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024, the expenditure limit started at $3,000,000 and phased out over a $40,000,000 range between $10,000,000 and $50,000,0002. Unassociated CCPCs calculate this limit under subsection 127(10.2) on Schedule T2SCH31, whereas associated CCPCs calculate and allocate the group expenditure limit under subsection 127(10.21) on Schedule T2SCH49 (Agreement Among Associated Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations to Allocate the Expenditure Limit)2.
2. The Gross Revenue Method (Mandatory for ECPCs; Elective for CCPCs — Subsections 127(10.6), 127(10.31) and 127(10.32))

Because public corporations and capital-intensive private companies frequently carry substantial equity or debt on their balance sheets (which inflates taxable capital employed in Canada even when corporate revenues are modest), Bill C-15 introduced a gross revenue phase-out structure under subsection 127(10.6)2. This method is mandatory for Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) and is available by election on a prescribed form to any CCPC under subsection 127(10.31) (CCPCs not associated with another corporation) or subsection 127(10.32) (associated CCPCs)2. If a CCPC belongs to an associated group and chooses the revenue method, all CCPCs in the associated group must jointly elect to use this method2.

Under subsection 127(10.6), the $6,000,000 expenditure limit decreases on a straight-line basis when the corporation's (or consolidated/associated group's) average annual gross revenue over the 3 preceding fiscal years lies between $15,000,000 and $75,000,0002:

Expenditure limit = $6,000,000 × [($60,000,000 − A) ÷ $60,000,000], where A is $0 if the 3-year average annual gross revenue is ≤ $15,000,000, and A is the lesser of $60,000,000 and the amount by which that average exceeds $15,000,000 if the 3-year average annual gross revenue exceeds $15,000,0002. For ECPCs that are members of a consolidated group preparing consolidated financial statements, the expenditure limit is shared among group members using the annual revenue reflected in those consolidated financial statements2. For an associated group of electing CCPCs, total average annual revenue must include: (1) financial statement revenues for each group member for the preceding 3 fiscal years, regardless of whether the corporations were associated throughout that entire period; (2) each corporation's reasonable share of annual revenue from any partnership or trust in which it held an interest; and (3) reasonable adjustments, such as eliminating intra-group sales of goods or services, so that the associated group reflects a single economic entity2.
1.5 Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures (Section 37) and Loss Restriction Events

As detailed in the CRA's Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures Policy (updated March 27, 2026), the Section 37 pool operates as a cumulative tax account calculated on Part 3, Section C of Form T66123. A taxpayer carrying on a business in Canada may deduct expenditures for SR&ED carried on in Canada that relate to a business of the taxpayer; under subsection 37(1.1), when a corporate claimant performs SR&ED related to a business actively engaged in by a related corporation (for example, a wholly owned R&D subsidiary performing research for a parent manufacturing corporation), the SR&ED is deemed to relate to the claimant's business23. Furthermore, under subsection 37(1.3), SR&ED performed in Canada's Exclusive Economic Zone is deemed to be performed in Canada23. Conversely, under subsection 37(4) and Regulation 2902(c), no deduction or ITC is permitted for expenditures made to acquire rights in, or arising out of, SR&ED (Halak v. Minister of National Revenue, 89 DTC 531)23.

The Section 37 pool is increased each taxation year under subsection 37(1), paragraphs (a) through (c.3) by: current SR&ED expenditures in Canada under paragraph 37(1)(a) (salaries or wages including permissible foreign SR&ED wages under subsection 37(1.5), materials consumed or transformed, equipment lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024, arm's length and non-arm's length SR&ED contracts performed on the claimant's behalf, third-party payments under subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(i.1) to (iii), and—under the Traditional Method only—directly related and incremental overhead expenditures); capital SR&ED expenditures under paragraph 37(1)(b) for depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024; repayments of government or non-government assistance under paragraph 37(1)(c) that previously reduced the pool; prior-year negative pool income inclusions under paragraph 37(1)(c.1) (arising via paragraph 12(1)(v)); pool balances transferred upon an amalgamation or wind-up; and prior-year recaptured SR&ED ITCs (and partnership ITC recapture excess amounts) under paragraphs 37(1)(c.2) and (c.3)6. Under the Proxy Method, the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) is never added to the Section 37 pool18.

Conversely, the Section 37 pool is decreased each taxation year under subsection 37(1), paragraphs (d) through (h) by: government or non-government assistance under paragraph 37(1)(d) that the claimant has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive on or before the filing-due date in respect of SR&ED expenditures in the pool; provincial "super-allowance benefit amounts" under paragraph 37(1)(d.1); SR&ED ITCs applied and/or refunded in the preceding taxation year under paragraph 37(1)(e); amounts deducted from the Section 37 pool in preceding taxation years under paragraph 37(1)(f); amounts deducted in respect of insolvency under section 61.3 in preceding years under paragraph 37(1)(f.1); and reductions triggered by a loss restriction event under paragraph 37(1)(h) and subsection 37(6.1)23.

Two structural restrictions govern corporate reorganizations and partnerships. First, under subsection 37(6.1), if control of a corporate claimant is acquired (or a trust acquires a new majority-interest beneficiary), a loss restriction event occurs and the pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures is reduced to nil at that time, subject to reinstatement in subsequent taxation years only if the specific business to which the expenditures related continues to be carried on for profit or with a reasonable expectation of profit, and only to the extent of income from that same business or a similar business23. Second, under paragraph 96(1)(e.1) and the CRA's SR&ED Claims for Partnerships Policy, a partnership is strictly prohibited from carrying forward an amount in its Section 37 pool to a subsequent fiscal period; the entire balance of the partnership's deductible SR&ED expenditure pool at year-end must be deducted in computing the partnership's net income for tax purposes for that year23.
2. Scientific and Technological Eligibility Framework ("Why" and "How" Methodology)
2.1 Subsection 248(1) Statutory Definition: Basic Research, Applied Research, and Experimental Development

The foundational threshold for any federal or provincial R&D tax claim in Canada is whether the underlying activities satisfy the statutory definition of "scientific research and experimental development" in subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act26. Subsection 248(1) defines SR&ED as a "systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis" and that falls into one of four eligible categories (paragraphs (a) through (d)), while explicitly excluding seven commercial and routine activity categories (paragraphs (e) through (k))26:

items: Paragraph 248(1)(a) — Basic Research: Work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view26.
Paragraph 248(1)(b) — Applied Research: Work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view26.

Paragraph 248(1)(c) — Experimental Development: Work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products or processes, including incremental improvements thereto10. Across Canadian industry, experimental development conducted within commercial operations and facilities accounts for the majority of corporate SR&ED claims19.

Paragraph 248(1)(d) — Support Work: Work undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer with respect to engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research, where the work is commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of work described in paragraph (a), (b), or (c) that is undertaken in Canada by or on behalf of the taxpayer8.

body.text: 2.2 The CRA Two-Step Eligibility Methodology: The "Why" and "How" Requirements

On August 13, 2021, the CRA replaced its earlier eligibility policy documents with the consolidated Guidelines on the eligibility of work for scientific research and experimental development (SR&ED) tax incentives26. The 2021 Guidelines structure the statutory requirements of subsection 248(1) around two core requirements—the "Why" requirement and the "How" requirement—both of which must be satisfied for work to qualify as SR&ED3.
Step 1: The "Why" Requirement (Scientific or Technological Advancement and Uncertainty)

The "Why" requirement examines the purpose of the work: it must be conducted for the advancement of scientific knowledge (basic or applied research) or for the purpose of achieving a technological advancement (experimental development)3. The central objective must be generating or discovering new conceptual knowledge—such as theories, predictive models, or technological know-how that advances the understanding of science or technology—rather than gathering routine factual measurements or data3. New knowledge is required only when the claimant faces a scientific or technological uncertainty, meaning it is uncertain whether a given result or objective can be achieved, or how to achieve it, due to an insufficiency in the available scientific or technological knowledge base (which encompasses both internal business knowledge and publicly available sources)19.

As outlined in the CRA Guidelines, characteristics of problems that indicate available technological knowledge is insufficient include situations where existing design methods are not applicable, requirements or specifications do not conform to existing standards, there are too many variables or unknowns, operating parameters or conditions lie outside normal ranges, the nature of the problem is evolving, data is lacking, interlocking constraints block standard solutions, or technological uncertainties arise from attempting to achieve commercial or economic cost targets19. Importantly, acquiring knowledge or know-how that already exists—such as through training, on-the-job learning, hiring expert employees or consultants, or purchasing proprietary knowledge—does not satisfy the requirement of attempting to achieve a technological advancement26. Conversely, success or failure in achieving the technical or commercial objective is irrelevant: because the "Why" requirement is governed strictly by the purpose of attempting to generate knowledge that resolves a scientific or technological uncertainty, an investigation that proves a technical hypothesis cannot work still advances technological understanding and qualifies as SR&ED21.
Step 2: The "How" Requirement (Systematic Investigation or Search)

The "How" requirement governs the methodology of the work: it must be a systematic investigation or search carried out in a field of science or technology (excluding social sciences and humanities) by means of experiment or analysis performed by qualified individuals26. To satisfy the "How" requirement under the CRA Guidelines, the claimant's process must encompass four sequential elements26:

items: Generating an Idea or Hypothesis: Formulating an idea consistent with known facts that serves as a starting point for further investigation toward achieving the objective or resolving the technological problem (expressed as a possible solution, proposed method, or approach)26.

Testing by Experiment or Analysis: Testing the idea or hypothesis by means of physical experiment or mathematical/computational analysis, where the hypothesis can evolve and change as a result of testing26.
Developing Logical Conclusions: Formulating logical conclusions based on the results or findings of the experiment or analysis26.
Keeping Contemporaneous Evidence: Maintaining evidence and documentation generated as the work progresses to substantiate the hypotheses, tests, and conclusions3.

body.text: 2.3 Paragraph 248(1)(d) Support Work vs. Paragraphs 248(1)(e)–(k) Statutory Exclusions

A central point of verification in CRA technical reviews is distinguishing between eligible Support Work under paragraph 248(1)(d) and Excluded Work under paragraphs 248(1)(e) to (k)26. Support work is never SR&ED on its own; if a business performs only engineering, design, or computer programming without an underlying basic research, applied research, or experimental development core under paragraphs (a), (b), or (c), none of the work qualifies26. However, once eligible core SR&ED work is undertaken in Canada, work within the eight statutory categories of paragraph 248(1)(d) becomes eligible if it is commensurate with the needs and directly in support of that core SR&ED26. By contrast, paragraphs 248(1)(e) through (k) enumerate seven categories of excluded work that can never be claimed26. As the CRA Guidelines explain, the key factor that distinguishes eligible support work from excluded work is purpose: why was the work performed—was it carried out specifically to perform the SR&ED, or for commercial/routine operations?26

body.text: 2.4 Special Operational Contexts: SR&ED During Production Runs, Commercial Assets, and Software/AI Development

Because most Canadian SR&ED claims arise within commercial facilities rather than standalone research laboratories, the CRA enforces specialized policies—specifically the SR&ED During Production Runs Policy and the SR&ED while Developing an Asset Policy (both updated July 19, 2016)—to separate commercial operations from eligible experimental development19.

When experimental trials are conducted on a commercial manufacturing line alongside or during commercial production runs (shop-floor SR&ED), the claimant must isolate the incremental expenditures attributable to the SR&ED work18. Any production output beyond what is strictly required for the SR&ED is defined in the CRA SR&ED Glossary as "excess production" and is excluded under paragraph 248(1)(i)42. Similarly, when SR&ED is performed while developing an asset—such as a prototype, pilot plant, custom product, or commercial asset—component parts physically incorporated into a custom product or commercial asset resulting from SR&ED can be claimed as materials transformed, but if those materials or resulting assets are subsequently sold or converted to commercial use, the ITC recapture rules under subsections 127(27) to (36) apply27. Furthermore, for depreciable capital property acquired after December 15, 2024 that is used in the development of an asset, the expenditure qualifies as an ASA (≥90%) SR&ED capital expenditure only if the property has minimal life expectancy (less than 10%) after its involvement in asset development, has limited residual value (less than 10%) after its involvement in asset development, or continues to be used in the performance of other SR&ED27.

In the software, financial technology, and artificial intelligence sectors, the CRA and the Federal Court of Appeal (National R&D Inc. v. Canada, 2022 FCA 72) require claimants to define the SR&ED project at the level of the specific interrelated activities necessary to resolve the technological uncertainty, rather than claiming an entire commercial software development project32. While developing novel payment rails, fraud detection algorithms, risk modelling architectures, or machine learning algorithms can qualify for SR&ED where standard computer science methods fail, resolving discrete coding problems within the known constraints of existing technologies or frameworks is disallowed as routine software engineering48.

body.text: While the PPA is initially calculated in Part 5, Section B of Form T661 as 55% of the Proxy Salary Base under subsection 2900(4) of the Regulations, claimants must also verify the Overall Cap on the PPA under subsection 2900(6) of the Regulations18. As set out in the CRA's Prescribed Proxy Amount Policy (updated April 28, 2022), the overall cap on the PPA is calculated using the formula A − B − C, where deductions specifically identified by the Regulations—such as Capital Cost Allowance (CCA), the SR&ED deduction claimed on Line 411 of Schedule T2SCH1, building rent, and interest expenses—are subtracted from total business deductions so that the notional PPA cannot exceed the remaining pool of general business expenses30.
3.2 Salaries and Wages, Specified Employee Caps (5x and 2.5x YMPE), Unpaid Remuneration, and Foreign Labour

Salaries and wages represent the primary expenditure category in Canadian SR&ED claims and are governed by subsection 248(1), subsections 37(8) and 37(9.1) to (9.5), subsection 78(4), and Regulation 2900, as interpreted in the CRA's SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy (updated January 28, 2025) and Prescribed Proxy Amount Policy25.

Under subsection 248(1), "salary or wages" means the income of a taxpayer from an office or employment as computed under subdivision a of Division B of Part I of the ITA25. For employees other than specified employees, allowable SR&ED salary or wages include basic salary and wages, vacation pay, statutory holiday pay, sick leave pay, pay in lieu of termination notice, tips or gratuities, honorariums, director's or management fees, commissions, bonuses, remuneration based on profits, inducement and non-competition payments, and taxable benefits under section 6 of the Act (either cash outlays or non-cash benefits where the value is a reasonable estimate of actual costs, excluding any GST/HST or PST for which an input tax credit or rebate is claimed under subsection 248(16), and provided the actual costs are not also claimed as a business expense)25. Conversely, the CRA strictly excludes from SR&ED salary or wages: (1) the employer's share of payroll-related benefits (which can only be claimed as overhead on Line 360 under the Traditional Method); (2) extended vacation or sick leave; (3) employee stock option benefits under section 7 (because issuing shares does not represent an expenditure incurred by the corporation); and (4) retiring allowances under subparagraph 56(1)(a)(ii) (which are excluded from salary or wages, though potentially eligible as overhead under the Traditional Method if directly related and incremental)25.

Under the Proxy Method, only the salary or wages of employees directly engaged in hands-on SR&ED in Canada may be claimed, determined by the actual tasks performed rather than the employee's job title8. Under the Traditional Method, salaries or wages of employees who directly undertake, supervise, or support the performance of SR&ED (other than those directly engaged), as well as clerical and administrative staff providing a direct and incremental service to SR&ED employees, may be claimed on Line 360 as overhead18. Under subsection 2900(5) of the Regulations, if a directly engaged employee spends all or substantially all (ASA, ≥90%) of their time in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada, 100% of their eligible salary or wages is included30.
Specified Employees and the Dual Statutory Caps (5 × YMPE and 2.5 × YMPE)

Under subsection 248(1) and section 251 of the ITA, a "specified employee" is an employee who is a specified shareholder (owning, directly or indirectly, at any time in the year, 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the corporation or a related corporation) or who does not deal at arm's length with the employer (such as a spouse, sibling, or other related person of a controlling shareholder)25. Specified employees are subject to three strict statutory restrictions25:

items: Disallowance of Bonuses and Profit-Based Remuneration: Bonuses and remuneration based on profits cannot be included as allowable SR&ED salary or wages for specified employees25. Furthermore, under subsection 2900(9) of the Regulations, bonuses, remuneration based on profits, section 6 taxable benefits, section 7 stock options, and prior-year unpaid wages paid in the current year (Line 310) are excluded from the Proxy Salary Base for all employees, whether specified or non-specified30.

Cap 1 — Maximum Allowable SR&ED Salary or Wages (5 × YMPE, Subsection 37(9.1)): The maximum SR&ED salary or wages expenditure that can be claimed for a specified employee is limited to 5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) (as determined under section 18 of the Canada Pension Plan for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends), prorated by the number of days in the taxation year on which the individual is a specified employee25. Where a specified employee works for two or more associated corporations, the aggregate total salary or wages claimed across all associated corporations cannot exceed 5 × YMPE, and the allocation must be documented using Form T1174 (Agreement Between Associated Corporations to Allocate Salary or Wages of Specified Employees for Scientific Research and Experimental Development [SR&ED])4.

Cap 2 — Maximum Proxy Salary Base (75% of Total Salary or 2.5 × YMPE, Regulation 2900(7) and 2900(8)): Under subsection 2900(7) of the Regulations, the amount that a claimant can include in the Proxy Salary Base for a specified employee is restricted to the lesser of30: (a) 75% of the specified employee's total salary or wages (SR&ED and non-SR&ED combined, excluding bonuses, remuneration based on profits, taxable benefits, and prior-year unpaid wages paid in the year); or (b) 2.5 times the YMPE for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends, prorated by the number of days in the taxation year that the claimant employed the individual (with no proration for time during the year that the employee was not a specified employee): 2.5 × YMPE × (number of days in the taxation year that the claimant employed the individual ÷ 365)30. Under subsection 2900(8), this proxy salary base ceiling is also capped once across an associated corporate group30.

Under subsection 78(4) of the ITA, employee remuneration that is not paid within 180 days from the end of the taxation year in which the expense was incurred is deemed not to have been incurred in that taxation year for SR&ED purposes25. Instead, it is treated as incurred only in the subsequent taxation year when actually paid (reported on Line 310 of Form T661), and under Regulation 2900(9) it never enters the Proxy Salary Base30. Similarly, under subsection 127(26), any current non-wage SR&ED expenditure incurred in the taxation year that remains unpaid 180 days after the end of the taxation year must be deducted from qualified SR&ED expenditures for that year; it can be added back in the subsequent taxation year in which it is paid (at 100% for materials/overhead or 80% for arm's length contracts) only if the unpaid amount was formally identified on Form T661 on or before the 18-month SR&ED reporting deadline for the original taxation year24.

Under subsection 37(1.5) of the ITA and Section 10.0 of the SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy, a claimant may claim permissible salary or wages for SR&ED work carried on outside Canada equal to the lesser of Amount A and Amount B23. Amount A is the total salary or wages paid for SR&ED work outside Canada that meets five mandatory criteria: (1) the work was directly undertaken by an employee of the claimant, not a contractor; (2) the employee was a resident of Canada at the time the expense was incurred; (3) the work related to a business of the claimant; (4) the foreign work was an integral part and solely in support of SR&ED carried on in Canada (any dual-purpose activity supporting both Canadian SR&ED and foreign SR&ED or non-SR&ED work is disqualified); and (5) the salary or wages were not subject to income or profits tax imposed by another country25. Amount B is 10% of the total salary or wages claimed for SR&ED carried on in Canada (Line 306 of Form T661; under the Traditional Method, Amount B can also include wages of employees who directly undertake, supervise, or support SR&ED claimed on Line 360, but cannot include clerical or administrative overhead staff wages on Line 360)5. On Form T661, permissible foreign wages are allocated between Line 307 (non-specified employees) and Line 309 (specified employees), such that Line 307 + Line 309 ≤ 10% × Line 30625.
3.3 Subcontractor Expenditures (Arm's Length 80% Rule vs. Non-Arm's Length Transfers) and Third-Party Payments

Under the CRA's Contract Expenditures for SR&ED Performed on Behalf of a Claimant Policy (updated March 30, 2022), when a claimant contracts with an arm's length performer to carry out SR&ED in Canada on the claimant's behalf, 100% of the allowable contract expenditure enters the claimant's Section 37 deductible pool, but only 80% of the allowable SR&ED contract expenditure qualifies for the Investment Tax Credit (for all expenditures incurred after 2012)33. To qualify for the payer's ITC, the SR&ED work must be performed in Canada by a taxable supplier24. Furthermore, if an arm's length performer is contracted to perform support work only under paragraph 248(1)(d) (directly in support of and commensurate with core SR&ED performed in Canada by or for the payer), the payer may claim the contract expenditure, but the arm's length contractor cannot claim an SR&ED credit because support work on its own does not meet the definition of SR&ED34. If the arm's length contractor performs core SR&ED (basic research, applied research, or experimental development), the contractor may claim its expenditures, but must reduce its qualified expenditures by the "contract payment" received from the payer33.

When a claimant enters into an SR&ED contract with a non-arm's length (NAL) performer, the payer's contract outlay is an allowable deduction in the Section 37 pool, but is not a qualified expenditure for ITC purposes (yielding $0 automatic ITC to the payer)34. An anti-avoidance rule also prevents claimants from circumventing the NAL restriction by inserting an arm's length intermediary between the payer and a NAL subcontractor if the main purpose of the arrangement was to obtain a qualified expenditure34. Instead, the NAL performer claims its own underlying SR&ED expenditures (including support-only work under the NAL exception in Section 7.4 of the policy), and the intercompany amount received from the NAL payer is not treated as a "contract payment" that reduces the NAL performer's qualified expenditures34. Under subsection 127(13) of the ITA, the NAL performer may transfer all or a portion of its qualified SR&ED expenditures (up to the contract amount) to the NAL payer by jointly filing Form T1146 (Agreement to Transfer Qualified Expenditures Incurred in Respect of SR&ED Contracts Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length)4.

By contrast, third-party payments are governed by the CRA's Third-Party Payments Policy (updated March 30, 2022) and subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(i.1) to (iii) of the ITA50. Unlike an SR&ED contract—where the payer controls the SR&ED work, holds exclusive rights, and claims expenditures on an accrual basis as the work is performed—a third-party payment gives the payer non-exclusive (preferential) entitlement to exploit the results of SR&ED conducted by an approved entity or Canadian resident corporation34. Like arm's length contracts, 80% of an eligible third-party payment qualifies for the SR&ED ITC, and the claimant must attach a completed Form T1263 (Third-Party Payments for SR&ED) for each payment18. Payments in kind are valued at fair market value (provided without conditional payments back to the claimant), and third-party payments used to acquire a building, a leasehold interest in a building, or building rental expense are excluded under paragraph 37(8)(d)61.

body.text: 3.4 Materials Consumed or Transformed, Overhead Allocations, Cloud Computing, and Prescribed Expenditures

Under the CRA's Materials for SR&ED Policy (updated December 18, 2014), Regulation 2900(2)(a) (Traditional Method), and subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(V) (Proxy Method), a claimant may claim 100% of the cost of materials consumed (destroyed or rendered virtually valueless during SR&ED) or materials transformed (physically altered or incorporated into another product or asset during SR&ED) in Canada35. To qualify as "materials for SR&ED", the raw materials, substances, or items must be physical and tangible (in a solid, liquid, or gaseous state) and must, at a given moment in the SR&ED process, compose the body of a tangible object on which SR&ED is being carried out or that results from the SR&ED35. Cost means laid-down cost for purchased items (invoice price, duties, freight, storage) or production cost for internally manufactured items, and materials can only be claimed in the taxation year in which they are actually consumed or transformed in Canada (with non-arm's length purchases restricted to the supplier's cost excluding profit)35. Items that do not compose the body of the physical object under investigation are excluded from materials, including petri dishes, beakers, flasks, pipettes, cleaning supplies, CDs/DVDs, used lubricants, utility or boiler feed water (unlike process water that enters a chemical product), and energy/utilities such as electricity, natural gas, propane, and ambient heat35. Under the Traditional Method, laboratory glassware and incremental utilities may be claimed as overhead on Line 360; under the Proxy Method, they are covered by the 55% PPA35.

Under the CRA's SR&ED Overhead and Other Expenditures Policy (updated October 14, 2022 / December 22, 2022) and Regulation 2900(2)(c) and 2900(3), overhead and other expenditures can be claimed only under the Traditional Method (on Line 360 of Form T661) and must satisfy two cumulative tests: (1) the "Directly Related" test, requiring a direct linkage with no intervening step to the SR&ED work, SR&ED staff, or machinery/equipment used in SR&ED, supported by rational allocation records; and (2) the "Incremental" test, requiring that the expenditure would not have been incurred had the prosecution of SR&ED not occurred50. Fixed costs—such as monthly telephone, cellular, or standard Internet service plans, and fixed-cost maintenance contracts—fail the incremental test and do not qualify (only incremental long-distance charges or directly related and incremental utilities, in-Canada training, Canadian testing travel, clinical study volunteer fees, health and safety expenses, and employee relocation expenses for SR&ED staff qualify, whereas headhunter fees, hiring advertisements, interview travel, and immigration/work permit costs are excluded as regular business expenses)18. As noted in the CRA's SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy (updated June 8, 2026), software licences may be treated as an SR&ED capital expenditure or a current lease expenditure depending on the specific contractual facts, while dedicated telecommunications bandwidth qualifies even under the Proxy Method as an equipment lease under Data Kinetics Ltd. v. Her Majesty the Queen, 98 DTC 187736.

Finally, under Section 2902 of the Income Tax Regulations, certain outlays are designated as "prescribed expenditures" and are excluded from qualified SR&ED expenditures (earning no ITCs, subtracted on Line 532 of Form T661) even if directly related and incremental under the Traditional Method24. Prescribed expenditures include fees for preparing SR&ED claims, costs to attend conventions or conferences, interest and financing expenses, general business administration or management expenses (legal, accounting, advertising, selling, entertainment, membership dues, fines/penalties), acquisitions of rights in or arising out of SR&ED, and the acquisition or refurbishment of used capital property6.
3.5 Restored Capital Expenditures, Shared-Use Equipment (SUE), Equipment Leases, and ITC Recapture

Pursuant to Bill C-15 (Royal Assent March 26, 2026) and the CRA's updated SR&ED Capital Expenditures Policy (updated June 29, 2026), SR&ED Shared-Use Equipment Policy (updated May 22, 2026), and SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy (updated June 8, 2026), the 2014–2024 repeal of capital and lease expenditures has been reversed for property acquired and lease costs incurred after December 15, 20246:

items: SR&ED Capital Expenditures (Line 390 of Form T661 — Paragraph 37(1)(b)): Depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024 that has become available for use under subsection 37(1.2) qualifies as an SR&ED capital expenditure if, at the time the expenditure was incurred, the claimant intended either that the property would be used during all or substantially all (ASA, ≥90%) of its operating time over its expected useful life in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada, or that ASA (≥90%) of its value would be consumed in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada6. Claimants must list the names of the 10 most expensive SR&ED properties acquired after December 15, 2024 for each project on Lines 262 and 263 of Form T661, and must not include Line 390 properties on Schedule T2SCH8 (Capital Cost Allowance)6. Non-depreciable property (such as land or inventory), buildings, and leasehold interests in buildings are excluded, and under the Proxy Method, General Purpose Office Equipment or Furniture (GPOEF) is also excluded6. Used depreciable property meeting the ≥90% ASA test is entered on Line 390 and included in the Section 37 deductible pool, but is excluded from earning the SR&ED ITC as a prescribed expenditure on Line 5326. Furthermore, because capital expenditures are eligible after December 15, 2024, the pre-December 16, 2024 "capital look-through rule" (which required reducing contract and third-party payments by the performer's non-current capital or lease costs) no longer applies to expenditures incurred after December 15, 202427.

Shared-Use Equipment (SUE — Line 504 of Form T661, Subsection 127(9)): When new depreciable equipment acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024 does not meet the ≥90% ASA test (and is not GPOEF or "Prescribed Depreciable Property" [PDP] under Regulation 2900(11)), it remains in its regular CCA class on Schedule T2SCH8 but can qualify for SR&ED ITCs on Line 504 as Shared-Use Equipment based on its actual operating time6. If the new equipment is used primarily (more than 50% and less than 90%) of its operating time for SR&ED in Canada during the First Period (from acquisition until the end of the first taxation year ending at least 12 months after acquisition), it qualifies as First-Term SUE and 1/4 (25%) of its capital cost is included in qualified expenditures for ITC purposes9. Provided it qualified as First-Term SUE, if it is used primarily (>50%) for SR&ED in Canada during the Second Period (from acquisition until the end of the first taxation year ending at least 24 months after acquisition), it qualifies as Second-Term SUE and an additional 1/4 (25%) of its capital cost qualifies for the ITC9. Under Regulation 2900(11), equipment is excluded as PDP if, at the time of acquisition, the claimant intended to use it for SR&ED during the assembly, construction, or commissioning of a commercial facility, plant, or line and intended to use it over its expected useful life primarily for non-SR&ED purposes9. Any ITC earned on SUE and applied or refunded reduces the Undepreciated Capital Cost (UCC) of the regular CCA class in the subsequent taxation year9.

Equipment Lease Expenditures (Post-December 15, 2024): Under the Traditional Method, equipment lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024 are claimed at 100% if the equipment is used ≥90% (ASA) of its operating time in SR&ED, or claimed proportionally on Line 360 as overhead if used <90% of the time in SR&ED (and directly related and incremental)6. Under the Proxy Method, equipment lease costs (excluding GPOEF) are claimed at 100% if used ≥90% (ASA) of operating time in SR&ED, at 50% if used more than 50% but less than 90% ("primarily") of operating time in SR&ED (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(VI)), and at 0% if used 50% or less of operating time in SR&ED36. Building rent remains excluded unless the building is a prescribed special-purpose building approved by the Department of Finance under Regulation 2903, while land leases after December 15, 2024 can qualify as overhead under the Traditional Method only36.

Recapture of Investment Tax Credits (Subsections 127(27) to 127(36)) and Deemed CCA Recapture (Line 440): If SR&ED capital property, shared-use equipment, or materials transformed (including animals, growing things, or components incorporated into prototypes or commercial assets) that earned an ITC are subsequently sold or converted to commercial use, subsections 127(27) to (36) of the ITA and the CRA's Recapture of SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy trigger an ITC recapture into Part I tax payable, alongside a recapture of deemed CCA on Line 440 of Form T661 for capital property deducted under paragraph 37(1)(b)6. By contrast, for materials allowed as cost of materials consumed (not incorporated into an SR&ED product), no recapture occurs unless proceeds received (such as insurance proceeds) exceed 10% of the cost of the materials29.

body.text: 4. Government Assistance, Contract Payments, and Federal Innovation Ecosystem Stacking
4.1 Statutory Grind Mechanics for Government Assistance, Non-Government Assistance, and Contract Payments

Under paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsections 127(18) to (20) of the ITA, as detailed in the CRA's Assistance and Contract Payments Policy (updated December 18, 2014), both the Section 37 pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures and qualified SR&ED expenditures for ITC purposes must be reduced by any government assistance, non-government assistance, or contract payments in respect of SR&ED that the claimant has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive on or before the income tax return filing-due date for the taxation year24.

Government assistance is defined in subsection 127(9) as assistance from a government, municipality, or other public authority—whether as a grant, subsidy, forgivable loan, deduction from tax, investment allowance, or any other form of assistance—excluding the federal SR&ED ITC itself33. Explicitly included as government assistance are all provincial and territorial R&D tax credits (unless validly renounced/waived) and direct federal grants such as NRC IRAP contributions33. Non-government assistance encompasses inducements, reimbursements, contributions, or allowances received from non-public entities under paragraph 12(1)(x), while contract payments encompass amounts paid or payable by an arm's length taxable supplier (or by a Canadian government, municipality, public authority, or Part I tax-exempt entity) for SR&ED to be performed for it or on its behalf33.

Reductions for assistance are applied on a project-by-project basis: assistance for one project reduces that project's SR&ED expenditures down to nil (any excess over the project's Section 37 pool expenditures is included in income rather than reducing unrelated projects)33. Furthermore, if a claimant uses the Proxy Method, government or non-government assistance that relates specifically to overhead expenditures (which are represented by the PPA and not included in the Section 37 pool) does not reduce the Section 37 pool33.
4.2 Forgivable Loans, Excluded Loans, Repayments of Assistance, and Non-Arm's Length Allocations (Form T1145)

Where a government funding agreement provides that repayment is conditional upon profits or revenues earned from the project (even if framed as royalties) or exempts repayment until revenues reach a specified threshold, the CRA treats the contribution as a forgivable loan (and therefore government assistance that reduces the Section 37 pool and qualified expenditures)33. However, effective January 1, 2020 (for loans made after December 31, 2019), subsection 12(11) of the ITA defines an "excluded loan", which is excluded from the definition of government assistance42.

When a claimant subsequently repays government or non-government assistance, the repayment increases the Section 37 pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures under paragraph 37(1)(c) (to the extent the assistance previously reduced the pool) and earns an SR&ED ITC calculated using the ITC rate from the taxation year in which the assistance was originally applied24. Because repayments of assistance are not strictly defined as current-year "qualified expenditures", the resulting ITC is non-refundable in the year of repayment, though it can reduce Part I tax payable, carry back 3 years, or carry forward 20 years24. Finally, when assistance or contract payments received by a non-arm's length (NAL) party exceed that recipient's qualified expenditures on a project, subsection 127(19) and (20) require allocating the excess across NAL group members performing the SR&ED using prescribed Form T1145 (Agreement to Allocate Assistance for SR&ED Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length), accompanied by a corporate resolution and filed by the transferor's filing-due date (or within the statutory Notice of Objection period)4.
4.3 Stacking SR&ED with NRC IRAP, Strategic Response Fund (formerly SIF), and Clean Technology ITCs

Canadian businesses frequently combine federal SR&ED tax credits with direct federal R&D grants and clean technology investment tax credits, subject to program stacking rules (typically capping total government assistance at 75% of eligible project costs) and the subsection 127(18) SR&ED reduction rules20:

items: National Research Council of Canada — Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC IRAP): Administered by the National Research Council of Canada through Industrial Technology Advisors (ITAs), NRC IRAP provides non-repayable, cost-shared contributions to incorporated, for-profit Canadian SMEs with 500 or fewer full-time employees (excluding sole proprietorships and partnerships)41. Unlike SR&ED, IRAP requires pre-project approval before eligible expenses begin63. According to Canadian grant advisory data (such as GrantCompass and GovMoney), standard IRAP reimburses up to 80% of internal R&D labour and a share of Canadian subcontractor costs (with typical SME awards ranging from $50,000 to $500,000, clean-tech and mid-market project caps up to $1,000,000–$10,000,000, and a $244.2 million Defence Industry Assist stream announced in January 2026 for SMEs developing dual-use technologies)20. When stacking IRAP with SR&ED, only the unreimbursed portion of expenses (plus the 55% PPA calculated on the gross directly engaged SR&ED salary base under the Proxy Method) remains in net qualified SR&ED expenditures33. For instance, in a worked stacking example from GrantCompass for a $500,000 clean-tech R&D project ($250,000 eligible labour, $50,000 other R&D expenses, and $200,000 clean-tech equipment purchase), an 80% IRAP grant on labour covers $200,000, the 35% enhanced SR&ED ITC on the remaining $300,000 of R&D expenses (including proxy/overhead) covers $105,000, and the 30% Clean Technology ITC on the $200,000 equipment purchase covers $60,000, leaving a net company cost of just $135,000 (73% total government coverage)63.

Strategic Response Fund (formerly the Strategic Innovation Fund [SIF]) and ISED Programs: Administered by Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada (ISED), the $5 billion Strategic Response Fund replaced the Strategic Innovation Fund (SIF) to support large-scale R&D and industrial commercialization projects (typically with a $10 million-plus project floor)20. Any grant or forgivable loan portion received from ISED or regional development agencies (such as FedDev Ontario, PrairiesCan, PacifiCan, ACOA, or CED) for SR&ED activities reduces the federal Section 37 pool and qualified expenditures33.

body.text: 5.1 Quebec: Abolition of Legacy Credits and the New CRIC Regime (Effective Post-March 25, 2025)

As confirmed by Revenu Québec and the Gouvernement du Québec, for taxation years and partnership fiscal periods beginning after March 25, 2025, Quebec replaced its legacy R&D tax credits with the consolidated Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC)10. Specifically, Quebec eliminated the former Tax Credit for Salaries and Wages (R&D) (RD-1029.7-V), the Tax Credit for University Research or Research Carried Out by a Public Research Centre or a Research Consortium (RD-1029.8.6-V), the Tax Credit for Private Partnership Pre-Competitive Research (RD-1029.8.16.1-V), the Tax Credit for Fees and Dues Paid to a Research Consortium (RD-1029.8.9.03-V, subject to a transition rule allowing cumulative fees/dues balances at the end of a fiscal period ending after March 25, 2025 to be claimed for taxation years ending no later than December 31, 2029), the Tax Credit for Technological Adaptation Services, the industrial design component of the Design Tax Credits, and the Tax Holiday for Foreign Researchers and Experts11.

The CRIC can only be claimed by corporations (and corporations that are members of a qualified partnership) that operate a business in Quebec, maintain an establishment in Quebec, and undertake (or cause to be undertaken on their behalf under contract) eligible R&D or pre-commercialization activities in Quebec10. To claim the CRIC, the corporation files Form RD-1029.8.CR-T (along with Form RD-222-V for the Quebec R&D expenditure deduction)10. While the R&D definition is harmonized with the federal SR&ED definition (with the CRA continuing to carry out the scientific review of R&D work), the CRIC also covers eligible pre-commercialization activities undertaken in conjunction with (and as a continuation of) R&D work carried out in Quebec by the corporation or on its behalf10. Eligible pre-commercialization activities consist of: (1) tests, technological validations, and studies carried out to meet regulatory requirements and aimed at obtaining an initial approval or certification for commercializing an innovation; and (2) product design, including the development of form and aesthetics, improved functionality, and choice of materials10.

Under the CRIC, qualified expenditures incurred in Quebec consist of: 100% of salaries and wages paid to employees for eligible R&D or pre-commercialization work; 50% of amounts paid to a subcontractor for a contract carried out in Quebec; 50% of payments made to an eligible public research centre, eligible research consortium, or eligible university entity; and 100% of capital property acquisition costs (excluding land, buildings, or a right to use land or buildings, and excluding property under a Large Investment Project tax holiday certificate)10. Unlike federal SR&ED, the CRIC does not provide a proxy overhead allowance71. Before applying the tax credit rate, total qualified expenditures must exceed an annual exclusion threshold, which equals the greater of $50,000 or the sum of the Basic Personal Amount of the Quebec personal income tax system for each eligible employee (prorated to reflect the percentage of time spent by each employee on eligible R&D and pre-commercialization activities; practitioner guides note the Quebec BPA is $18,571/$18,751 in 2025 and $18,952 in 2026)10. Regardless of corporate asset size or foreign ownership, the CRIC is 100% refundable at a rate of 30% on the first $1,000,000 of qualified expenditures above the exclusion threshold, and 20% on all qualified expenditures exceeding that $1,000,000 tier10.
5.2 Ontario: OITC (8%), ORDTC (3.5%), OBRITC (20%), and Compounding Phase-Out Mechanics
Corporations with a permanent establishment in Ontario carrying out SR&ED in Ontario can access three provincial credits administered by the CRA under the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario)68:

items: Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC — Schedule 566, 8% Refundable): Provides an 8% fully refundable credit on up to $3,000,000 of qualified Ontario SR&ED expenditures (maximum $240,000 annual credit)75. While the federal enhanced limit increased to $6,000,000 for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, Ontario retained its $3,000,000 OITC expenditure limit52. However, Ontario updated the OITC qualified expenditure rules to include 100% of qualified capital expenditures made on or after December 16, 2024 (whereas capital expenditures made after December 31, 2013 and before December 16, 2024 remain excluded)75. The $3,000,000 OITC expenditure limit is shared across associated corporations and phases out if the associated group's prior-year federal taxable income lies between $500,000 and $800,000 or if prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada lies between $25,000,000 and $50,000,00075. As practitioner guides (such as GovMoney) highlight, when both phase-out ranges apply simultaneously on Schedule 566, the two reductions compound multiplicatively: for example, a corporation with $700,000 of prior-year taxable income (leaving 1/3, or $1,000,000, of the $3,000,000 limit) and $30,000,000 of prior-year taxable capital (leaving 80% of the limit) receives an OITC expenditure limit of $1,000,000 × 80% = $800,000 (maximum OITC of $64,000)77.

Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC — Schedule 508, 3.5% Non-Refundable): Provides a 3.5% non-refundable credit (carryback 3 years, carryforward 20 years, no expenditure limit) to any non-exempt corporation with an Ontario permanent establishment68. Under Ontario law, the 8% OITC is government assistance that reduces the ORDTC expenditure base before the 3.5% rate is applied (whereas the ORDTC and the federal ITC do not reduce the OITC or ORDTC base)76. Thus, on $1,000,000 of Ontario qualified expenditures, the OITC is $1,000,000 × 8% = $80,000, and the ORDTC is ($1,000,000 − $80,000) × 3.5% = $920,000 × 3.5% = $32,200 (a combined Ontario credit of $112,200, or 11.22% of the eligible pool)76. Both the $80,000 OITC and the $32,200 ORDTC then reduce the federal qualified expenditure pool ($1,000,000 − $80,000 − $32,200 = $887,800), yielding a 35% federal refundable ITC of $310,73076. Under subsection 43(1) of the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario), a corporation in a tax loss position can formally waive the current-year ORDTC in whole or in part to avoid reducing its 35% cash-refundable federal ITC68.

Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC — Schedules 568 and 569, 20% Refundable): Provides a 20% fully refundable credit on up to $20,000,000 of qualified expenditures annually (maximum $4,000,000 refund) for eligible SR&ED contracts with approved Ontario universities, colleges, or hospital research institutes46.

body.text: 5.3 Western Provinces: British Columbia (10%), Alberta IEG (8%/20%), Saskatchewan ($2M Cap Reform), and Manitoba (15%)

In British Columbia, corporations with a BC permanent establishment claim the 10% BC SR&ED Tax Credit on Form T666 within a strict 18-month filing window from tax year-end1. The credit is 100% refundable for CCPCs up to the $3,000,000 expenditure limit (maximum $300,000 refund) and non-refundable above $3,000,000 or for non-CCPCs (carryback 3 years, carryforward 10 years)62. In Alberta, corporations claim the 100% refundable Innovation Employment Grant (IEG) on AT1 Schedule 29 and Form AT4970 within 15 months after the AT1 filing-due date, earning an 8% payment on eligible Alberta R&D spending up to the corporation's base level of spending (the average eligible R&D spending over the preceding 2 years) and an enhanced 20% payment on eligible spending exceeding that 2-year base level, up to a $4,000,000 annual spending cap62.

In Saskatchewan, under the CRA's updated guidance (October 28, 2026) for Schedule T2SCH403, the 10% Saskatchewan R&D Tax Credit is 100% refundable for CCPCs on the first $2,000,000 of eligible expenditures for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024 (doubled from the $1,000,000 limit that applied to taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024), while CCPC expenditures above $2,000,000 and non-CCPC expenditures earn a 10% non-refundable credit (carryback 3 years, carryforward 10 years, or waivable under subsection 63.4(13)), up to a combined annual credit cap of $1,000,00012. In Manitoba, corporations claim the 15% Manitoba R&D Tax Credit on Schedule T2SCH380 (within 1 year after the T2 filing-due date), where half of the credit (7.5%) is refundable and half (7.5%) is non-refundable (carryback 3 years, carryforward 20 years) for in-house R&D, and the full 15% is refundable for R&D conducted under contract with a qualifying institute62.
5.4 Atlantic Provinces (Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Newfoundland and Labrador) and Yukon (15%/20%)

Across Atlantic Canada, Nova Scotia (T2SCH340), New Brunswick (T2SCH360), and Newfoundland and Labrador (T2SCH301 for corporations; T1129 for individuals) each provide a 15% fully refundable R&D tax credit with no expenditure limit62. Notably, in Newfoundland and Labrador, provincial eligible expenditures are not reduced by government or non-government assistance (except for GST/HST input tax credits), although the NL credit itself still reduces the federal SR&ED pool62. In the Yukon, corporations with a Yukon permanent establishment claim a 15% fully refundable credit on Schedule T2SCH442 (within 18 months of tax year-end), plus an additional 5% refundable credit (for a 20% total credit) on eligible expenditures paid or payable to Yukon University82.

6.1 Institutional Governance: CRA Coordinating Tax Services Offices, Department of Finance, and Revenu Québec

The federal SR&ED program and eight of the ten provincial/territorial R&D tax credit regimes are administered by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA), while legislative policy is formulated by the Department of Finance Canada, Quebec's CRIC is administered financially by Revenu Québec (with the CRA conducting the scientific review of R&D activities), and Alberta's IEG is administered by Alberta Tax and Revenue Administration (TRA)8. Within the CRA, technical eligibility is evaluated by Research and Technology Advisors (RTAs) reporting to a Research and Technology Manager (RTM), while expenditure allowability and ITC calculations are audited by Financial Reviewers (FRs) reporting to a Financial Review Manager (FRM)84.

body.text: 6.2 Voluntary Pre-Claim Approval Process (Launched April 1, 2026) and Mandatory FTCAS

On April 1, 2026, the CRA launched the formal, optional SR&ED Pre-Claim Approval process, enabling eligible businesses to obtain an upfront determination from the CRA within 8 weeks on whether their planned projects meet the definition of SR&ED before work begins or costs are incurred8. To qualify for Pre-Claim Approval, a business must operate in Canada, have less than $25,000,000 in annual gross business income, be a CCPC, other Canadian corporation, or partnership, and be in good standing with the CRA, and its proposed projects must not involve issues currently under objection or litigation13. A business first requests a case number on Canada.ca (received in My Business Account within 2 business days for existing claimants, or via a CRA phone call within 5 business days for new claimants), submits the application form (Part 1 General Information, Lines 010–012; Part 2 Project Information, Sections A to D, Lines 020–060) and supporting project plans through My Business Account for up to 3 projects, and meets with an SR&ED specialist13. If granted, Pre-Claim Approval is valid for up to 3 years, and if a subsequent refundable SR&ED claim containing only pre-claim approved projects is selected for expenditure review, the CRA service standard is cut in half from 180 days to 90 days13.

Separately, under the First-Time Claimant Advisory Service (FTCAS) (updated January 20, 2026), claimants submitting their first SR&ED claim or those that have not filed an SR&ED claim in the preceding 3 years may be selected after filing for a mandatory virtual advisory meeting with CRA SR&ED officers86. The FTCAS session is strictly educational—no eligibility determinations or adjustments are made to the submitted claim during the FTCAS meeting, any expected refund is processed after the meeting concludes, and the claimant receives a tailored written advisory report to support future claims86.
6.3 Statutory Filing Deadlines (18-Month Rule), Prescribed Forms, and Form T661 Line-by-Line Architecture

Under subsections 37(11), 37(11.1), 37(12), paragraph 127(9)(m), and subsection 220(2.2) of the ITA, as set out in the CRA's SR&ED Filing Requirements Policy (updated January 28, 2025), a claimant must file Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31 (for corporations) or Form T2038(IND) (for individuals and trusts) containing the prescribed information on or before its SR&ED reporting deadline, which is 12 months after the income tax return filing-due date for the taxation year4. For corporations (whose T2 return is due 6 months after year-end), the reporting deadline is 18 months after the end of the taxation year; for individuals (whose T1 business return is due June 15 of the following year), the reporting deadline is 17.5 months after the calendar year-end (June 15 of the second following year)4. Under subsection 220(2.2), the CRA has no legal authority to extend the SR&ED reporting deadline: if prescribed forms containing prescribed information are not filed on time, the expenditures are permanently barred from Section 37 deduction and earn no ITCs4. (Only Part 9 claim preparer disclosures, deductions of pre-existing Section 37 pool balances, and ticking additional evidence boxes on Lines 270–282 during a review are exempt from the 18-month deadline)4.
