body.text: 6.4 Part 9 Claim Preparer Disclosures, Contingency Fee Arrangements, and Civil Penalties

Under paragraph 37(11)(b) and subsections 162(5.1), 162(5.2), and 162(5.3) of the ITA, Part 9 of Form T661 must be completed for each claim preparer that has accepted consideration to prepare or assist in the preparation of the SR&ED claim (reporting the preparer's identity, Business Number, billing arrangement code from the Part 9 table—such as contingency fee, hourly rate, or flat fee—and fee details)4. If no external claim preparer assisted, the claimant completes only Lines 935, 970, and 97521.

If prescribed information in Part 9 is missing, incomplete, or inaccurate, a $1,000 penalty may be assessed under subsection 162(5.1), for which the claimant and the claim preparer are jointly and severally (or solidarily) liable under subsection 162(5.2)4. However, the SR&ED claim itself will not be disallowed solely because Part 9 information is missing, incomplete, or inaccurate4. Separately, overstated SR&ED claims made knowingly or under circumstances amounting to gross negligence are subject to penalties under the CRA's Gross Negligence Penalty on Overstated SR&ED Claims Policy (updated January 28, 2025, formerly Application Policy SR&ED 96-05)6.
6.5 CRA Technical and Financial Review Process, Service Standards, Administrative Review (Form RC532), and Objections

For complete refundable SR&ED claims, the CRA adheres to three service standards (which it commits to meeting 90% of the time): 60 calendar days for claims accepted as filed; 90 calendar days for refundable claims selected for review that only include projects granted Pre-Claim Approval; and 180 calendar days for all other refundable claims selected for review86.
When a claim is selected for review, the CRA follows the three-step procedure in The SR&ED Review Process: A Guide for Claimants (updated April 20, 2026)85:

items: Step 1 — Start of the Review: The assigned RTA or FR telephones the claimant to explain the issues and projects under review, confirm official language preference, and schedule a virtual (or, exceptionally with management approval, on-site) review meeting, followed by an initial letter and meeting agenda85. Under the Standard Timelines for Information Requests, pre-meeting document requests generally carry a 30-day deadline85.

Step 2 — The Review Meeting and Information Requests: The RTA and FR interview the technical and financial personnel who performed and tracked the work, conduct a virtual tour of the premises/equipment, review contemporaneous evidence (Lines 270–282 of Form T661), and share preliminary findings85.

Step 3 — End of the Review (Proposal Package and 30-Day Response Window): If adjustments are proposed, the CRA sends a Proposal Package containing the SR&ED Project Eligibility Report, a Proposal Letter detailing expenditure/ITC adjustments and any proposed penalties, and financial schedules85. The claimant has 30 calendar days to submit written representations and additional evidence before the Notice of Assessment/Reassessment is issued84.

body.text: If disagreements arise during the review before the file is closed, the CRA's Guidelines for Resolving Claimants' SR&ED Concerns (updated December 5, 2025) establish a three-step dispute resolution hierarchy: Step One is talking directly to the RTA and/or FR; Step Two is escalating to the Research and Technology Manager (RTM) and/or Financial Review Manager (FRM); and Step Three (available after receiving the Proposal Package and before the 30-day proposal period expires and the file is closed) is filing Form RC532 with the National SR&ED Administrative Review Intake Centre to request an Administrative Review by the local SR&ED Assistant Director84. The Assistant Director checks whether due process was granted and whether the review complied with SR&ED legislation and policies, issuing a decision either maintaining the finding or ordering it reconsidered84.

Once a Notice of Assessment or Reassessment is issued, the claimant has 90 calendar days to file a formal Notice of Objection (online via My Business Account / Represent a Client, or by mail using Form T400A or Form RC592) with the CRA Appeals Branch (large corporations with >$10,000,000 in taxable capital must specify each issue and exact dollar relief sought and pay 50% of disputed tax)86. If the CRA Appeals Branch confirms the assessment (or after 90 days without a decision), the claimant has 90 days to appeal to the Tax Court of Canada, 30 days (excluding July and August) to appeal a TCC judgment to the Federal Court of Appeal, and 60 days (excluding July) to seek leave to appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada86.
7. Landmark Canadian SR&ED Jurisprudence and Evidentiary Precedents
7.1 The Foundational Five-Criteria Test: Northwest Hydraulic, RIS-Christie, and C.W. Agencies

Across Canadian jurisprudence—reaffirmed by the Federal Court of Appeal in National R&D Inc. v. Canada, 2022 FCA 72 and Tuna Temple Inc. v. Canada, 2026 FCA 175—the authoritative legal test for establishing SR&ED under subsection 248(1) of the ITA is the five-criteria test set out by Justice Bowman in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520, 1998 CanLII 553 (TCC) at paragraph 16, approved by the Federal Court of Appeal in RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen, [1999] 1 C.T.C. 132, 99 DTC 5087 (FCA) at paragraph 10, and summarized in C.W. Agencies Inc. v. Canada, 2001 FCA 393 at paragraph 1748:

items: Technological Risk or Uncertainty: Was there a technological risk or uncertainty which could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures?48
Formulation of Hypotheses: Did the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulate hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty?48
Accordance with the Scientific Method: Did the procedure adopted accord with the total discipline of the scientific method including the formulation, testing and modification of hypotheses?48
Technological Advancement: Did the process result in a technological advancement?48
Contemporaneous Records: Was a detailed record of the hypotheses tested, and results kept as the work progressed?48

body.text: 7.2 Judicial Supremacy Over Administrative Guidelines and Expert Witness Standards: Kam-Press and National R&D

In Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Canada, 2021 FCA 88, and National R&D Inc. v. Canada, 2022 FCA 72 (affirming 2020 TCC 47), the Federal Court of Appeal held that it is the exclusive role of the courts to interpret the Income Tax Act, and in National R&D it held that the CRA's August 2021 "Why" and "How" eligibility guidelines did not remove the requirement to follow the scientific method or alter the Northwest Hydraulic five-criteria test47. In National R&D, the FCA upheld the disallowance of a software development claim where, despite establishing a technological uncertainty, the developer failed to systematically formulate, test, and record hypotheses48. Furthermore, the FCA affirmed the exclusion of the taxpayer's expert witness report, holding that expert witnesses owe an overriding duty of impartiality to the Tax Court, must not act as advocates or opine on the ultimate legal issue of SR&ED eligibility, and cannot be used to introduce unsworn factual evidence through the back door51.
7.3 Contemporaneous Documentation, Qualified Personnel, and Contextual Uncertainty: Joel Theatrical, Canafric, and Tuna Temple (2026 FCA 175)
Four additional judicial principles govern audit defence and litigation before the Tax Court of Canada:

items: Admissibility of Testimonial Evidence Alongside Documentary Records (RIS-Christie, 99 DTC 5087 [FCA] and Formadrain Inc. v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 42): As noted by the TCC in National R&D (2020 TCC 47 at paras. 65–66), citing RIS-Christie (at paras. 14–15) and Formadrain (at para. 94), the fifth criterion (detailed records kept as work progressed) is not explicitly mandated by the wording of the ITA to be exclusively documentary, and oral testimonial evidence is legally admissible; however, failing to maintain contemporaneous documentary records creates severe evidentiary risk at trial48.

Competent Engineering Baseline vs. Trial-and-Error (Joel Theatrical Rigging Contractors (1980) Ltd. v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 6): In Joel Theatrical Rigging, the TCC dismissed claims for a motorized fire curtain descent project and a manual override project where none of the claimant's personnel held an engineering degree or P.Eng. designation or consulted a professional engineer during the experiments, leaving the Court with no reliable evidence that the problem could not have been resolved by routine mechanical engineering89.

Contextual Uncertainty with Known Ingredients and Practical Lab Logs (Canafric Inc. v. The King, TCC, July 26, 2023): In Canafric, Justice Bodie allowed a food manufacturer's appeal for developing a room-temperature shelf-stable vinegar-based beverage, holding that: (1) a technological uncertainty can exist even when using preservatives known to competent professionals in the field, provided the solution has never been used in that specific product context; and (2) contemporaneous documentation is meant to keep track of hypotheses generated, experiments undertaken, and results obtained, and does not need to be formatted for an outsider unfamiliar with the field to replicate the results15.

Appellate Standard of Review (Tuna Temple Inc. v. Canada, 2026 FCA 175): In Tuna Temple, the Federal Court of Appeal reaffirmed the five Northwest Hydraulic / C.W. Agencies criteria and held that a Tax Court judge's factual findings on whether a taxpayer's activities met those criteria cannot be overturned on appeal absent a palpable and overriding error91.
